seo.title: ReportAI — From voice note to report, explained from the inside
seo.description: An AI agent that turns the voice note from a site visit into the report of a Word template. Real demo, interactive architecture (LangGraph, Pydantic, Postgres, Gotenberg) and design decisions.

hero.eyebrow: Case study · an AI agent with a human in the loop
hero.subheadline: ReportAI turns the voice note from a site visit into the report of a Word template, ready to approve and send. This page shows how it is built, with the real system: from audio to PDF.
hero.note: Built end to end: backend, agent, panel and deployment. Source code public on GitHub.

realDemo.paragraph: A site inspection, dictated and run through the real system: transcription, extraction and the filled-in template. Nothing was touched up afterwards, not even the transcript's typos. Press play.

useCases.heading: One engine, any template.
useCases.sub: The system knows nothing about safety inspections: it knows schemas. Each document type is configuration, a list of fields and a Word file with tags, not code.

safetyVisit.title: Safety visits and inspections
safetyVisit.body: Issues with who is responsible, the corrective action and the deadline, work stopped and notes. It is the demo’s template.

incident.title: Incidents and accidents
incident.body: What happened, where, how serious it is and what was already done. Dictated on the spot and reviewed calmly.

custom.title: Whatever gets filled in by hand today
custom.body: Maintenance work orders, checklists, minutes. An assistant reads the Word file and proposes the fields; they only need correcting.

differentiator.heading: The problem: the report gets written at night.
differentiator.paragraph: The visit is notes in a notebook and photos on a phone, and the report is typed into Word at the end of the day. It is repetitive work where data gets lost along the way: a deadline, who is responsible. Exactly what an agent with validation and human approval can do well.

templateFidelity.heading: The template is data, not code.
templateFidelity.paragraph: The company uploads the Word file it already uses, with its logo and format. An assistant proposes which fields it has and where each goes; they are corrected, previewed as a PDF with sample data and activated. When the document is generated, docxtpl replaces each tag with its value, so the result is the company’s own, not a generic PDF with a logo pasted on top.
templateFidelity.check: Without a template of its own there are starters: site safety inspection, work order, visit report and incident report.

approval.heading: A human in the loop, for real.
approval.paragraph1: Every report reaches the chat as a draft first. If a required field is missing, such as the deadline for an action, the bot asks and the graph waits for the answer. If something is off, it is corrected by replying and generated again.
approval.paragraph2: The channel is Telegram: each technician talks to the company’s bot like to any contact. Whoever approves can also review, correct and approve from the panel.

architecture.heading: From voice note to report, inside the system.
architecture.sub: Five stages, one path. Pick one to see what it does, how it does it and what leaves the server.
architecture.hintPinned: Scroll: the data moves on its own. You can also click a stage.
architecture.hintTabs: Click a stage or use the arrow keys.

dictate.name: Dictate
dictate.plain: You send a voice note on Telegram, the way you would to any contact. With photos if you want.
tech: Telegram notifies the server through a webhook. If the installation has no public address, the worker polls Telegram instead.
Every message is deduplicated by its id: a Telegram retry never creates two reports.
The report and its queued job are created in one Postgres transaction: both exist or neither does.
dictate.why: A Postgres queue, no Redis or broker: on someone else’s server every extra piece is a support call. A job is claimed with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and a lease; if the worker dies, another one picks it up.
dictate.data: The message travels through Telegram, like any chat. Nothing else.

transcribe.name: Transcribe
transcribe.plain: The audio becomes text, in Spanish or English, with the configured speech service.
tech: A Whisper model behind any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (/audio/transcriptions). By default, whisper-large-v3-turbo on Groq.
temperature 0 and the company’s language as a hint: repeatable output, and English speech is not transcribed as if it were Spanish.
If the job is cut midway, it resumes from its last saved point instead of transcribing again.
transcribe.why: An OpenAI-compatible endpoint instead of a vendor SDK: switching provider means changing a URL and a key, not the code.
transcribe.data: The audio goes to the configured speech provider, with the company’s key. It is the only step that sends it.

extract.name: Fill the fields
extract.plain: The model reads the transcript and fills the template’s sections. What was not said stays empty: nothing is invented.
tech: A LangGraph graph with typed Pydantic state: each stage is a node and each decision a conditional edge.
The schema is built at runtime from the template’s fields and requested from the model as structured output. Every filled field carries the literal quote it came from, checked against the transcript.
If validation fails, the error goes back to the model and it retries, with a cap. If a required field is missing, the graph pauses and the bot asks.
extract.why: Empty (null) beats invented. In a formal document, a plausible date nobody said is worse than a gap: a missing required field is asked for, never filled in.
extract.data: The transcript goes to the configured AI model (Claude or another), with the company’s key.

approve.name: You approve
approve.plain: The draft arrives in the chat. You confirm, correct it with a voice note or text, or cancel. Nothing leaves without your approval.
tech: The graph stops at LangGraph’s interrupt() and its state is saved in Postgres: it can wait for hours and survives a restart.
An “ok” or a 👍 is settled by rules, without calling the model. A long reply is classified by the model and, when unsure, it counts as a correction, never as an approval.
A correction goes back to extraction with whatever is added, with a retry cap. It can also be reviewed and approved from the panel.
approve.why: An agent should not send anything on someone else’s behalf without a human checkpoint. Here it is an edge of the graph, not a warning in the interface.
approve.data: With the buttons or an “ok”, nothing leaves. Only a long reply goes to the model to be classified.

deliver.name: Deliver
deliver.plain: The Word template is filled and converted to PDF. It reaches the chat and, by email, whoever is configured, and it is kept in the history.
tech: docxtpl fills the template’s .docx with the approved fields, in an isolated Jinja2 environment with autoescaping: “Smith & Sons” does not break the document.
Gotenberg (LibreOffice) converts the .docx to PDF in a container on the server itself.
Each copy, the chat and every email, is a row in the delivery log: if one fails, only that one is retried.
deliver.why: One delivery per copy: if an email fails, the chat is not resent and the PDF is not generated again.
deliver.data: Only what is sent leaves: the PDF over Telegram and through the configured mail server.

impact.heading: The problem, in numbers.
impact.sub: A field technician spends hours turning visits into Word documents. Move a team’s numbers and see what changes. The starting values are assumptions of the model, not measurements.

stats.gross: Value of the time, per month
stats.running: AI and server cost, per month

impact.live: {hours} hours freed per month: €{net} net per year.
how: Reports per month = technicians × reports per week × weeks per year ÷ 12.
Hours freed = reports × (minutes today − minutes with ReportAI) ÷ 60.
Value of the time = hours freed × cost per hour.
Net = value of the time − (reports × AI cost + server).
impact.disclaimer: The starting values are assumptions of this model, not results measured with customers. AI is estimated at cents per report (the demo cost under 3 cents) and the server at about €9 a month. It does not include setup or maintenance costs.

graph.q: Why a graph and not a single prompt?
graph.a: Because the flow has state and pauses: it waits for a human reply, asks for what is missing, retries and resumes after a restart. With LangGraph each step is a node with typed state and each decision an explicit edge, so every transition can be tested and reasoned about.

queue.q: Why a Postgres queue and not Redis or Celery?
queue.a: Because each installation lives on a company’s server and every extra piece is support. Postgres is already there: the worker claims jobs with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, a lease and retries with growing waits. The cost is a lower throughput ceiling than a dedicated broker: fine for visit reports, not for thousands of events per second.

hallucination.q: How is the AI kept from making data up?
hallucination.a: In layers. The model returns null for what was not said. Every filled field comes with the literal quote, checked against the transcript. Pydantic validates types and formats: a date has to be a date. If a required field is missing, the bot asks. And nothing leaves without human approval. No layer is perfect; together they bound the risk.

crash.q: What happens if the server dies halfway through a report?
crash.a: Each job has a lease that a heartbeat renews. If the worker dies, the lease expires and another worker picks the job up, and the report resumes from the last LangGraph checkpoint in Postgres, without repeating the transcription or the extraction. A deploy stops the worker gracefully: it finishes the job in hand.

providers.q: How do you switch AI provider?
providers.a: AI is configuration, not code. There are two adapters: Anthropic with native structured output, and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint with function calling. Transcription is a separate setting, on an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Each company brings its own keys.

newdoc.q: How is a new document type added?
newdoc.a: It is configuration: a list of fields with their type (text, number, date, time, email, phone, list, enum, table or photo) and a Word file with tags. The Pydantic schema is built at runtime from that list, so there is no code to touch and nothing to redeploy.

limits.a: Telegram is the official channel and WhatsApp is in testing. One installation serves one company. The languages are Spanish and English. And extraction quality depends on the model chosen and on how well the visit is dictated.
